newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia steel firm seen attractive with govt aid.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia steel firm seen attractive with govt aid.

text.p: Malaysia's assumption of 2.9 billion ringgit ($1.15 billion) in losses racked up by Perwaja Steel Sdn Bhd should make the troubled national steel firm more attractive to prospective investors, analysts said on Thursday.

"This will make it become more attractive for whoever's taking it over," said Audrey Ho, head of research at Mohaiyani Securities. Almost half Perwaja's equity is held by the government, with 51 percent owned by small steel company Maju Holdings Sdn Bhd.
Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad, the patron of the 10-year-old project, said on Wednesday that while the government would absorb Perwaja's losses, it will not pump new funds into the insolvent firm.

Nearly a year has passed since Perwaja was revealed to be in financial trouble. An anti-corruption agency is investigating alleged irregularities at the firm, whose former managing director Eric Chia resigned in August 1995.
Rescuers of Perwaja, which makes billets and long products, will have to inject more than a billion ringgit to revive the firm, the government has estimated.

Analysts said it was not surprising that the government has stepped in to back Perwaja, given its large vested interest. The state government in eastern Terengganu state, where Perwaja runs its billeting plant, has a 19 percent interest in the firm while the federal government owns 30 percent.

The government and local banks also hold large portions of Perwaja's debt, with 1.2 billion ringgit from the government, 2.5 billion with local banks and 3.1 billion with foreign financial institutions.
"It would be unfair if Perwaja were to palm off its losses to the bankers," said Muzni Mohamed, chief analyst at Nikko Advisory. "The loss being absorbed is a natural progression."
Though a medium-sized producer of steel in Malaysia, Perwaja's output is still critical for the rapidly growing country, analysts added.

Perwaja makes about 600,000 tonnes a year in billets versus largest producer Lion group's Amsteel Corp Bhd, which makes 750,000 a year. In long products, used for steel bars and in the construction industry, Perwaja turns out 450,000 tonnes a year, compared with Lion's 850,000 tonnes.
"If Perwaja stops, we would have a deficit," said J.M. Sassoon investment analyst Louie Ooi, who said steel is in high demand in the booming construction industry.

Estimated domestic demand for steel is 3.2 million tonnes a year, which is rising by about 15 percent annually. Total capacity is 3.6 million tonnes "but plants don't produce at 100 percent", Ooi said.

A shored-up Perwaja may attract investors to take up the government's equity stake in the future, analysts said. "I do not forsee the government's stake in the company being a long-term holding," Muzni said. "I believe there are still some bidders who are very keen on Perwaja."

Said an equity analyst at a local securities firm: "Some of the original parties who were to be involved in the rescue operations were scared off by the debts incurred." Maju Holdings has said it expects the steel maker to turn a net profit of 100 million ringgit by 1998.
Mahathir has expressed the government's determination to save the steel company. "Perwaja was my idea, if it fails, I will be embarrassed," he said in December.
